reproduction_number_range.source: Guerra et al. 2017, Lancet Infect Dis, abstract via Europe PMC: often cited 12 to 18, estimates vary more widely

transmissibility_per_day.source: Midpoint of the cited range (15) divided by the infectious days; not itself observed

case_fatality.source: Panum 1846 Faroe epidemic via Hektoen International (second hand): 170 deaths among 6100 infected, 2.8 percent; the higher figures for malnutrition and first-contact outbreaks are not from the source opened and are not modelled

immunity.source: Panum 1846 via Hektoen: no reinfection after 65 years

stage.incubating.source: Non-infectious part of incubation: rash about 14 days after exposure (range 7 to 21) less the 4 days of infectiousness before rash; CDC Pink Book chapter 13 seen only as search summaries. Shape 6 is a derived Erlang approximation

stage.infectious.source: Infectious from about 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset, CDC clinician materials as reported by search results, page text not opened

density_exponent.source: Wikipedia, Basic reproduction number (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_reproduction_number, opened): R0 = contact rate / recovery rate, the contact rate set by 'the number of susceptible people in the population that the infected people contact'; whether contact rises with density is not stated there. Chowell et al., 1918 influenza in England and Wales (PMC2596813, opened): 'we found no association between transmissibility, death rates and indicators of population density and residential crowding', R between 1.3 and 1.9, and deaths scaling as population to the power 0.71-0.77 in rural areas and about 1.0 in towns. So the exponent of contact on crowding lies between 0 (that study) and 1 (mass action, density-dependent contact); 0.5 is the midpoint, a ballpark. Rader et al. 2020 (Nature Medicine; search summary only, full text not opened): crowded cities have longer epidemics and larger attack rates.
